messages.subject: Justification of monotonic split approach
messages.body_plain:
Here's my understanding of monotonic splitting in GBM:

To find the optimal monotonically increasing split for a variable, we assume that if the mean pseudo-residual in the right node is less than the mean pseudo-residual in the left node, then the prediction at the right node will be greater than the prediction at the left node.

I believe this assumption does not hold for all distributions. For example, with the laplace distribution it's easy to construct a counter-example.

Has anyone written down the mathematics of monotonic splits in GBM?

Thanks!

Pat O'Reilly

messages.subject: github
messages.body_plain:
I have some updates, but am currently frustrated by github.  Can someone help set me straight.
It shouldn't be hard (survival has used sccs, rcs, svn, and mercurial in succession, so I
have experience.) but I'm missing something.  Likely something obvious.

The obvious flow is clone, branch, make changes, submit.

1. If I do this on my linux box, there seems to be no way to submit the changes back to
you all for review.

2. If I instead do 'fork' on github, clone that on linux, branch, push, then I can ask for
a pull on gitbub.  That's ok.  But then 3 weeks later if I want to do another change,
there is (near as I can tell) no "pull" command on the github site, no way to update that
copy.  Start again from scratch?  Really?
    Rerunning the whole chain loses any personal test files I developed on my copy.  (I
tend to have lots of these), and just seems to be out of sync with any long term
collaboration.

Terry T.

messages.subject: Re: github
messages.body_plain:
Ah, yes. git is (ahem) intuitive like that.

The workflow is clone as one off

Then branch, code, push to your repo, PR, back to master, fetch from gbm-developers/gbm, merge with gbm-developers/gbm/master, push to your master if you feel like it.

In what-to-type detail, what you should first do (as a one-off, in your clone)

git remote add upstream https://github.com/gbm-developers/gbm

Then, for each new thing.

git checkout -b patch/mynewstuff

Code code code, committing as nesc

git push -u origin/patch/mynewstuff

Pull request (and wait!)

git checkout master

git fetch upstream

git merge --ff-only upstream/master

For more advanced use with temporary local files I'm told that git stash is the thing to do, but I just get confused when I try that...

--
pdm
